title: Pityriasis rosea
summary: A self-limiting rash of young adults: a single herald patch, then oval scaly patches along skin lines on the trunk (‘Christmas tree’), fading over 6–12 weeks. Reassure, but test for syphilis when the picture is atypical.

glance.think: A single larger oval patch, then 1–2 weeks later many smaller pink oval patches with a collarette of scale on the trunk.
glance.engine: Probably reactivation of HHV-6/HHV-7; not contagious in practice.
glance.backbone: Explain and reassure; emollients, mild topical steroid or antihistamine for itch; review if it lasts beyond 12 weeks.
glance.never_miss: Secondary syphilis (palms and soles, mucosal lesions, lymph nodes), guttate psoriasis, tinea and drug eruptions; PR in early pregnancy (miscarriage risk).

what: **Diagnosis confirmed from the course case:** the case shows a single initial lesion (Picture 1) followed ~2 weeks later by a generalised eruption (Picture 2) after a URTI. The diagnosis is **pityriasis rosea**; guttate psoriasis was listed as a **differential**, not the answer. The key mimic to exclude is **secondary syphilis** as the must-not-miss differential.

A common, **self-limiting** papulosquamous eruption of adolescents and young adults (10–35 years), beginning with a single **herald patch** followed days to ~2 weeks later by a **secondary eruption** of smaller oval scaly patches on the trunk and proximal limbs. Lasts about **6–12 weeks** (most 6–8). Recurrence is uncommon (~2–3%).
cause: Cause not proven; strongest evidence links it to **reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and 7 (HHV-6/HHV-7)** — supported by preceding URTI/prodrome, seasonal clustering, and low recurrence. **PR-like (pityriasiform) drug eruptions** occur with e.g. ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, isotretinoin, gold, some biologics/vaccines — these lack a herald patch and persist while the drug continues.

list: Possible prodrome: malaise, headache, sore throat, low-grade fever (URTI — Case 3).
**Herald patch:** single, 2–5 cm, oval, salmon-pink (grey-brown/violaceous in darker skin) plaque with fine **collarette scale** inside the edge; often trunk, upper arm, neck, thigh.

**Secondary eruption** (after ~1–2 weeks): many smaller oval macules/plaques with collarette scale, long axes along skin cleavage lines → **"Christmas-tree" pattern** on the back, "V" on the chest; usually spares face, scalp, palms and soles.
Itch: none to moderate (~25% significant).
Variants: **inverse** (flexural — axillae/groin, commoner in children/skin of colour), papular, vesicular, purpuric, urticarial, giant, unilateral, oral lesions.
Darker skin: more papular/facial lesions; prolonged post-inflammatory hyper/hypopigmentation.
**Syphilis serology** (treponemal EIA ± RPR) if atypical, palms/soles involved, no herald patch, sexual risk, or lasting >12 weeks.
**Skin scrapings for mycology** if the herald patch alone looks like tinea (scale at advancing edge).
Drug history (pityriasiform drug eruption).
Biopsy rarely (atypical/persistent).
Pregnancy test/status relevant — see 3.6.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Many small (0.5–1 cm) **drop-like papules** with thicker **silvery scale** over the whole lesion, **no herald patch**, 1–3 weeks after **streptococcal sore throat**/tonsillitis; may have family history, nail pitting, scalp involvement; can persist/evolve into plaque psoriasis

**Palms and soles** copper-red papules, mucous patches, condylomata lata, patchy alopecia, generalised lymphadenopathy, malaise; papules **tender to blunt pressure (Buschke–Ollendorff sign)**; sexual history; positive serology
Annular, active scaly edge with central clearing, scale at advancing edge, often asymmetric; KOH/scraping positive
Coin-shaped, very itchy, crusted/oozing, limbs > trunk
New drug, larger lesions, no herald patch, persists, eosinophils on biopsy
Fine scale, hypo/hyperpigmented, upper trunk, Malassezia on scraping, chronic
Small red-brown papules with mica-like scale, recurrent crops over months

differentials: **Guttate psoriasis** is an acute eruption of small (<1 cm) drop-like scaly papules/plaques, typically in children, teens, and young adults — often **1–3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis**. Module 4 Spot Diagnosis consensus: widespread scaly eruption on trunk/limbs in a 14-year-old with no prior skin disease → **guttate psoriasis**. Main clinical DDx: **pityriasis rosea**.

list: Same psoriatic immune axis; strong link to **Group A streptococcus** and HLA-C*06:02-enriched early-onset disease.
May be first presentation of psoriasis or remain a one-off self-limited episode.
PR (DDx): putative viral trigger; herald patch then secondary oval plaques on Langer lines.

head: Guttate psoriasis
Pityriasis rosea
rows: Herald patch then smaller oval plaques with collarette
Weeks–months; may clear or evolve to plaque psoriasis

list: Clinical. Ask about sore throat; consider throat swab / ASO if indicated.
Look for herald patch and Christmas-tree pattern to favour PR.
Biopsy rarely needed.
Consider syphilis serology if PR-like but atypical (palms/soles, systemic, persistent).
Emollients; mild–potent TCS matched to extent/site; vitamin D analogues sometimes.
Treat proven strep infection per local antimicrobial guidance (treating strep does not always clear guttate quickly).
Counsel possible recurrence or later plaque psoriasis.
Reassure; emollient ± mild TCS for itch; UV advice individualised; refer if severe/atypical.
Teen + abrupt drop-like scaly rash + recent sore throat ≈ guttate until proven otherwise.
Avoid oral steroids.
Safety-net return if eruption becomes confluent, pustular, or erythrodermic.

management: Based on NICE CKS *Pityriasis rosea* and PCDS/BAD leaflet themes:

list: Explain benign, **non-contagious**, self-limiting (6–12 weeks); no isolation needed; scars do not occur (pigment change may persist months in darker skin).
Emollients and soap substitutes; avoid hot showers, perfumed products, tight clothes; moderate sun exposure may speed resolution in some.

Itch: emollient ± **mild–moderate topical corticosteroid** (e.g. clobetasone butyrate 0.05%) short course to itchy areas; **sedating antihistamine** at night (e.g. chlorphenamine; counsel drowsiness) or non-sedating by day.
Evidence for **high-dose aciclovir** early in extensive/symptomatic disease is limited — specialist decision.

management.h: Guttate psoriasis (if that is the diagnosis instead)

list: Throat swab only if sore throat ongoing (treat streptococcal infection per NG84); emollients; topical vitamin D analogue ± topical steroid, coal-tar; refer dermatology for **NB-UVB phototherapy** if widespread/distressing (lesions too numerous for topicals). Often clears in 3–4 months; ~⅓ later develop chronic plaque psoriasis.
**Pregnancy:** PR in pregnancy (esp. first 15 weeks) has been associated with miscarriage/premature delivery — inform/refer to midwife/obstetrician (CKS).
Atypical features, palms/soles/mucosal involvement or sexual risk → **syphilis serology / refer to sexual health (GUM)**.
Persisting >12 weeks, diagnostic doubt, severe symptoms → GP/dermatology.
Suspected drug cause → review medication with prescriber.

red_flags: Palm or sole lesions, mouth ulcers, lymphadenopathy or sexual risk: **syphilis serology** and sexual-health referral.
Pityriasis rosea in the **first 15 weeks of pregnancy**: inform the midwife or obstetric team.
Lasting more than 3 months: reconsider the diagnosis.
pearls: "One big patch first, then many small ovals along the ribs" = PR; "shower of small drops after strep throat" = guttate psoriasis.
The herald patch is often mis-treated as ringworm — antifungal failure is a clue.
**Every generalised papulosquamous rash: ask about sexual history and look at palms and soles.**
Do not prescribe oral steroids for PR (may prolong/worsen).
Provide BAD/PCDS patient leaflet; review if not resolving by 3 months.
